elements.name: Tagged Union
elements.what: A data type whose value is exactly one of several named alternatives, carrying a tag that identifies which alternative is present.
elements.problem: Safely representing 'one of N shapes' data without unchecked casts or sentinel conventions; enables exhaustive case analysis so unhandled alternatives are caught statically.
elements.named_in: Types and Programming Languages - Benjamin C. Pierce (2002)

elements.name: Option Type
elements.what: A sum type with exactly two cases - a present value (Some/Just) or absence (None/Nothing) - making optionality explicit in the type.
elements.problem: Eliminates null-reference and sentinel-value failure modes by forcing every consumer to handle the absent case before touching the value.
elements.named_in: Haskell 98 Language and Libraries Report - Simon Peyton Jones, ed. (2003)

elements.name: Result Type
elements.what: A sum type carrying either a success value or an error value, returned instead of throwing, so failure is part of the function's signature.
elements.problem: Makes failure paths visible and composable in the type system, avoiding invisible exception control flow and forcing callers to acknowledge errors.
elements.named_in: The Rust Programming Language - Klabnik & Nichols (2019), 'Recoverable Errors with Result'

elements.name: Monad
elements.what: An interface (unit/return plus bind) for sequencing computations inside a context - optionality, failure, state, IO - so effectful steps compose like plain functions.
elements.problem: Gives one uniform composition law for wildly different effect plumbings, removing hand-written propagation of state, errors, or absence through call chains.
elements.named_in: Notions of Computation and Monads - Eugenio Moggi (1991)
elements.borderline: Umbrella abstraction: concrete instances (State, Reader, Writer, IO, monad transformers) are folded here as variants, not enumerated; kept because the interface itself is the recurring design element.

elements.name: Thunk
elements.what: A zero-argument closure standing in for a not-yet-computed value, forced (evaluated) on first demand and typically cached thereafter.
elements.problem: Defers expensive or possibly-unneeded computation until its result is actually demanded, enabling infinite structures, call-by-need semantics, and cheap short-circuiting.
elements.named_in: Thunks: A Way of Compiling Procedure Statements with Some Comments on Procedure Declarations - P. Z. Ingerman (CACM, 1961)

elements.name: Memoization
elements.what: Caching a function's results keyed by its arguments so repeated calls with the same inputs return the stored answer instead of recomputing.
elements.problem: Trades memory for time on pure or effectively-pure functions with overlapping call patterns (recursive decomposition, repeated queries), often turning exponential recursions polynomial.
elements.named_in: 'Memo' Functions and Machine Learning - Donald Michie (Nature, 1968)

elements.name: Persistent Data Structure
elements.what: A data structure whose update operations return a new version while old versions remain valid, sharing unchanged substructure between versions.
elements.problem: Provides safe sharing across threads and cheap history/undo without defensive copying, by making every version immutable and reusing common parts.
elements.named_in: Making Data Structures Persistent - Driscoll, Sarnak, Sleator, Tarjan (JCSS, 1989)

elements.name: Continuation-Passing Style
elements.what: Writing functions to take an explicit continuation - a callback receiving the result - instead of returning, making control flow a first-class value.
elements.problem: Reifies 'what happens next' so programs can implement early exit, backtracking, coroutines, and asynchronous flows in a language without those control features.
elements.named_in: Compiling with Continuations - Andrew W. Appel (1992)

elements.name: Trampoline
elements.what: A driver loop that repeatedly invokes returned thunks/step objects so that deep or mutual recursion runs in constant stack space.
elements.problem: Avoids stack overflow from deep tail or mutual recursion on runtimes without tail-call elimination by converting nested calls into iterated returns.
elements.named_in: Trampolined Style - Ganz, Friedman, Wand (ICFP, 1999)

elements.name: Defunctionalization
elements.what: Replacing first-class functions with a tagged-union of the closures that actually occur plus an apply function that dispatches on the tag.
elements.problem: Lets higher-order programs run (or be serialized, stored, or sent) in first-order settings - C, wire protocols, event logs - by turning behavior into data.
elements.named_in: Definitional Interpreters for Higher-Order Programming Languages - John C. Reynolds (1972)
elements.borderline: Charter-flagged: originated as a compiler/interpreter transformation, but is a recurring in-program design move (serializable jobs, state machines from closures), so it passes the altitude test.

elements.name: Lens
elements.what: A first-class, composable pair of getter and updater focused on a part of an immutable structure, so nested reads and copy-with-change updates compose like functions.
elements.problem: Removes the boilerplate of updating deeply nested immutable records, where each level otherwise requires manual copy-and-replace code.
elements.named_in: Combinators for Bidirectional Tree Transformations - Foster, Greenwald, Moore, Pierce, Schmitt (TOPLAS, 2007)

elements.name: Phantom Type
elements.what: A type parameter that appears in a type's signature but not in its runtime representation, used purely to encode compile-time distinctions or states.
elements.problem: Statically separates values that share a representation but must not mix (sanitized vs raw strings, units, protocol states) at zero runtime cost.
elements.named_in: Domain Specific Embedded Compilers - Leijen & Meijer (DSL '99, 1999)

elements.name: Smart Constructor
elements.what: A function that is the only exported way to build a value of an abstract type, performing validation or normalization so every constructed value satisfies the type's invariants.
elements.problem: Guarantees invariants at the construction boundary - hiding the raw data constructor makes invalid values unrepresentable to the rest of the program.
elements.named_in: Smart constructors - Haskell wiki (haskell.org)

elements.name: Effect Handler
elements.what: A construct that intercepts declared effect operations performed by a computation and decides how to interpret them and how to resume the suspended computation.
elements.problem: Separates what effects a computation performs from how they are implemented, enabling swappable interpreters, testing without mocks, and user-defined control flow (exceptions, generators, async).
elements.named_in: Handlers of Algebraic Effects - Plotkin & Pretnar (ESOP, 2009)
elements.borderline: Charter-flagged modern: still primarily a language/library research construct, but implemented in shipping languages (OCaml 5, Koka, Unison) and libraries, so it clears the establishedness gate.

elements.name: Functional Core, Imperative Shell
elements.what: Structuring a component as a pure decision-making core wrapped by a thin imperative layer that performs all IO and mutation.
elements.problem: Isolates hard-to-test effects at the boundary so the bulk of logic is pure, deterministic, and unit-testable without mocks.
elements.named_in: Functional Core, Imperative Shell - Gary Bernhardt (Destroy All Software screencast, 2012)
elements.borderline: Charter-flagged: a program-structuring statement that pulls toward architecture, but it is implementable inside one component and named/recurring, so kept in the design realm.

elements.name: Collection Pipeline
elements.what: Composing a sequence of collection-transforming operations (filter, map, reduce and kin) where each stage's output feeds the next.
elements.problem: Replaces tangled loop-and-accumulator code with declarative, reorderable stages, making data transformations readable and often lazily or parallelly executable.
elements.named_in: Collection Pipeline - Martin Fowler (martinfowler.com, 2014)

elements.name: Newtype
elements.what: A distinct nominal type wrapping exactly one underlying value, giving it a separate identity in the type system with little or no runtime cost.
elements.problem: Prevents mixing semantically different values that share a representation (UserId vs OrderId, meters vs feet) and provides an attachment point for domain-specific operations and instances.
elements.named_in: The Rust Programming Language - Klabnik & Nichols (2019), 'Using the Newtype Pattern'

elements.name: Typestate
elements.what: Encoding an object's protocol states as distinct types so that operations invalid in the current state do not type-check, with transitions returning the next state's type.
elements.problem: Moves 'called in the wrong order' protocol errors (use before open, double close, build before configure) from runtime checks to compile-time rejection.
elements.named_in: Typestate: A Programming Language Concept for Enhancing Software Reliability - Strom & Yemini (IEEE TSE, 1986)

elements.name: Zipper
elements.what: A representation of a position inside an immutable structure as the focused element plus its inverted surrounding context, allowing O(1) local edits and navigation.
elements.problem: Enables efficient localized updates and cursor-style navigation in purely functional trees and lists, where naive editing would rebuild the path from the root on every step.
elements.named_in: The Zipper - Gérard Huet (Journal of Functional Programming, 1997)

elements.name: Immutable Object
elements.what: An object whose observable state cannot change after construction; all 'modifications' produce new instances.
elements.problem: Eliminates aliasing bugs, defensive copies, and data races on shared state - immutable values are safe to share, cache, and use as keys.
elements.named_in: Patterns in Java, Volume 1 - Mark Grand (1998)

elements.name: Railway-Oriented Programming
elements.what: Composing a workflow as a chain of functions over a two-track success/failure type, where any failure switches the rest of the pipeline onto the error track automatically.
elements.problem: Keeps multi-step validation/IO workflows linear and readable while still short-circuiting on the first failure and accumulating error information, without nested conditionals or exceptions.
elements.named_in: Railway Oriented Programming - Scott Wlaschin (fsharpforfunandprofit.com / NDC, 2014)
elements.borderline: Essentially a named usage idiom of the result type (monadic bind); kept as a separate entry because the name is established and widely taught, cross-linked to result-type.

elements.name: Tagless Final
elements.what: Encoding an embedded language's operations as a parameterized interface (type class/trait) so programs are polymorphic terms interpretable by any implementation.
elements.problem: Allows multiple interpreters (evaluate, pretty-print, optimize) over the same program description and extension with new operations without reworking existing code, avoiding the tag-dispatch and expression-problem costs of a data-type encoding.
elements.named_in: Finally Tagless, Partially Evaluated - Carette, Kiselyov, Shan (JFP, 2009)
elements.borderline: Advanced FP-community pattern rather than broad-industry vocabulary; establishedness is solid (canonical paper, standard Scala/Haskell pattern name) so kept with honest tag.

elements.name: Parser Combinator
elements.what: Building parsers as first-class values composed with higher-order functions (sequence, choice, repetition), so the grammar is expressed directly as executable code.
elements.problem: Provides modular, testable, incrementally-buildable parsers inside the host language, avoiding external grammar files and generator build steps for mid-complexity input languages.
elements.named_in: Monadic Parser Combinators - Hutton & Meijer (1996)

elements.name: Embedded Domain-Specific Language
elements.what: A domain-specific vocabulary implemented as a library within a host language, reusing the host's syntax, types, and tooling instead of a separate parser.
elements.problem: Gives domain experts a notation close to their problem while inheriting the host language's abstraction, checking, and ecosystem - no separate compiler to build or maintain.
elements.named_in: Building Domain-Specific Embedded Languages - Paul Hudak (ACM Computing Surveys, 1996)
elements.borderline: Umbrella technique spanning many concrete idioms (fluent interfaces, combinator libraries, tagless final); kept because the name and canonical source are established and the mechanism is in-program.

elements.name: Functional Reactive Programming
elements.what: Programming with first-class time-varying values (behaviors/signals) and event streams composed declaratively, with the runtime propagating changes through the dependency graph.
elements.problem: Replaces manual observer wiring and callback state machines for time- and event-driven logic (UIs, animation, robotics) with composable declarative dataflow.
elements.named_in: Functional Reactive Animation - Elliott & Hudak (ICFP, 1997)
elements.borderline: A programming model verging on paradigm; kept because it is library-implementable inside one program (Yampa, reflex, Rx-style signal libraries) and canonically named. Overlaps concurrency/reactive scout - fine.

elements.name: Free Monad
elements.what: Representing a computation as a data structure of instructions (built from a functor) that is later run by separately-defined interpreters.
elements.problem: Decouples the description of an effectful program from its execution, enabling multiple interpreters (production, test, dry-run, logging) over one program value.
elements.named_in: Data Types à la Carte - Wouter Swierstra (JFP, 2008)
elements.borderline: Could be folded into the monad umbrella as a variant, but it names a distinct design move (reify program, interpret later) with its own literature, so kept as an entry.

parked_architecture.name: MapReduce
parked_architecture.why: System-scale data-processing topology built from functional primitives (Dean & Ghemawat 2004); fails the altitude test upward - it is a statement of system structure, not an in-component mechanism.

parked_architecture.name: Dataflow programming (as a system paradigm)
parked_architecture.why: As a whole-system execution paradigm/topology it is architecture-realm; the in-program design elements it decomposes into (collection pipeline, FRP) are cataloged here.

parked_architecture.name: Function-as-a-Service / serverless functions
parked_architecture.why: Deployment and topology construct ('functions' as unit of system decomposition); architecture realm, Phase 3.

excluded_notable.name: algebraic data type (ADT)
excluded_notable.why: DECISION LOG (charter-directed): NOT a separate umbrella entry. ADT = sum types + product types; the design element is tagged-union (which carries the sum side and the aliases); product/record types are raw language syntax. Recorded here so the decision is auditable.

excluded_notable.name: pattern matching
excluded_notable.why: Charter-directed exclusion: language syntax level (destructuring/case analysis feature), below the altitude band; it is the consumption syntax for tagged unions, noted there.

excluded_notable.name: fold / map / higher-order functions
excluded_notable.why: Charter-directed exclusion: syntax-level primitives; their design-level composition is captured by collection-pipeline.

excluded_notable.name: currying / partial application
excluded_notable.why: Language-level calling-convention technique, below the altitude band; not an in-program design mechanism in its own right.

excluded_notable.name: type class
excluded_notable.why: Language type-system feature (Wadler & Blott 1989, 'How to make ad-hoc polymorphism less ad hoc'), not an implementable in-program mechanism; the patterns built on it (tagless final, newtype instances) are cataloged.

excluded_notable.name: functor / applicative functor hierarchy
excluded_notable.why: Type-class abstraction ladder (McBride & Paterson 2008); monad is kept as the representative umbrella entry, the rest of the hierarchy is not enumerated per the one-element-per-mechanism rule.

excluded_notable.name: recursion schemes (catamorphism/anamorphism etc.)
excluded_notable.why: Meijer, Fokkinga & Paterson 1991 ('bananas' paper); generalized folds - theory/syntax altitude, and enumeration would open an algorithmics zoo owned elsewhere.

excluded_notable.name: parse, don't validate
excluded_notable.why: Principle/slogan (Alexis King, 2019), not a mechanism; its mechanism side is the smart-constructor entry.

excluded_notable.name: make illegal states unrepresentable
excluded_notable.why: Design principle (Yaron Minsky), not a mechanism; realized via tagged-union, newtype, phantom-type, typestate, smart-constructor entries.

excluded_notable.name: session types
excluded_notable.why: Type-system research feature for communication protocols (Honda 1993); language-level, not an in-program mechanism; the practical in-program cousin (typestate) is cataloged.

excluded_notable.name: pure function / referential transparency
excluded_notable.why: A semantic property, not a mechanism; the structural idiom that operationalizes it (functional core, imperative shell) is cataloged.

notes: Coverage: 26 elements across the charter list plus extensions (newtype, typestate, zipper, parser combinator, EDSL, FRP, tagless final, free monad, railway-oriented programming, immutable object). Decisions logged: (1) ADT is NOT a separate umbrella entry - tagged-union carries it (see excluded_notable); (2) monad kept as one borderline umbrella entry with the instance/transformer zoo folded in, free monad kept separately as a distinct design move; (3) lens entry absorbs the optics variants (prism, traversal). Cross-references: persistent-data-structure notes HAMT/finger-tree/banker's-queue variants belong to the sibling datastructures corpus (E:/dev/corpora/datastructures) - only the mechanism-level entry lives here. Known overlaps accepted per charter: collection-pipeline (poeaa/Fowler scout), immutable-object (OO scout), parser-combinator (parsing scout), FRP (concurrency scout), smart-constructor/EDSL (construction-api scout). Corpus work_ids.tsv contains no FP naming sources (no Okasaki, GoF-FP, Wadler, Reynolds, Haskell works), so all named_in_corpus_id are null - Phase 2 will need new nodes for Moggi 1991, Reynolds 1972, Okasaki 1998, Huet 1997, Hutton & Meijer 1996, Plotkin & Pretnar 2009, Foster et al. 2007, etc. Live spot-checks this session: Haskell wiki Smart constructors page (loaded), Leijen & Meijer DSL'99 (search-confirmed as the phantom-types source), Wlaschin ROP 2014 (search-confirmed). Thin spots: type-level programming beyond phantom/typestate (GADTs, refinement types, dependent types) deliberately excluded as language features; effect-system vocabulary beyond effect handlers is still research-fluid; Okasaki-style amortization techniques (lazy rebuilding, scheduling) left to the datastructures corpus.
